public_rationale: The evidence supports a substantial part of the claim: multiple model families repeatedly produce unsupported information on demanding tasks, and medical evaluations identify serious errors. It does not settle the full breadth or ordinary-use frequency implied by “essentially all” and “fairly regularly.” The inspected reputational fabrication is older than the target period. These gaps prevent a supported verdict on the whole proposition; they do not demonstrate that it is false.
limitations: Difficult and adversarial benchmarks cannot be treated as random samples of everyday use.
Models and safeguards change, so older incidents cannot establish current behavior by themselves.
A false accusation does not automatically satisfy the legal elements of defamation.

statement.excerpt: Because essentially all their software has a tendency to fabricate fairly regularly and even defame people and to sometimes give bad medical information, and so on.
statement.document_title: Maybe Section 230 doesn’t shield AI companies from liability, after all

our_interpretation: Read the scope as broad coverage of major LLM providers, rather than every individual model or software product.
Read recurring fabrication as a reproducible tendency in realistic uses, without inventing a numerical frequency threshold.
Read “defame” in its ordinary sense of false, reputation-damaging statements; a completed legal finding of defamation is not required.
For this ongoing technical claim, use the current-year evaluation period before publication: January 1 through June 11, 2026. No standard quarterly reporting cycle exists.
Older incidents provide context but cannot alone establish the state of current systems.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporary, sufficiently broad evaluations establish recurring fabrication across major providers, with documented reputationally harmful falsehoods and erroneous medical outputs.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative contemporary evidence establishes that recurring fabrication is not broadly present, or directly refutes the claimed categories of harmful output.

evidence.explanation: The February benchmark release reports substantial errors across proprietary and open-weight model families on difficult multi-turn legal, research, medical, and coding tasks. It supports recurring fabrication in those settings, but does not estimate ordinary-use frequency or establish every listed harm.

evidence.publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence.explanation: The March publication reports clinically relevant errors across evaluated models, including a 29.1% rate for its best performer. Its tests deliberately inject hallucination traps, and the accessible abstract does not date the underlying experiments; it is therefore supporting context rather than decisive evidence of current ordinary-use frequency.

evidence.locator: Section I, Pure Fabrication; discussion of Walters v. OpenAI
evidence.explanation: The summary describes ChatGPT inventing an embezzlement accusation against Mark Walters, but the incident predates the target period. It also explains that OpenAI won summary judgment, so fabricated reputational content must not be equated with established legal liability.

The paper finds meaningful variation across models and tasks and discusses much lower rates on easier evaluations. This limits extrapolation from its difficult benchmark to a general claim about frequency.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Dated, reproducible evaluations of contemporary models across the major providers, using representative tasks, together with authenticated reputational and medical falsehoods from the target period.
